title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling & Benchmark Playbook (2027-06-30)
author: Ava Lin
body:
Overview

This playbook consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling and benchmarking runbooks, release notes checklist, known issues catalog, and team wiki links for day-to-day operations. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, infra, and SRE teams who run, optimize, and troubleshoot the Redwood inference serving stack.

Contents
1. Runtime architecture overview
2. Kernel scheduling and policy guidance
3. Profiling playbooks (CPU/GPU/Memory/KV cache)
4. Benchmarking suite and test matrix
5. Release notes checklist for runtime changes
6. Known issues and mitigation patterns
7. Runbooks: critical operational procedures
8. Team wiki & onboarding links

1) Runtime architecture overview

Short summary:
- The Redwood serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine with four primary layers: Ingress/Router, Request Orchestration (batching & scheduling), Execution Engine (kernels & quantized paths), and Observability/Cache layer (prefix/KV cache + tracing).
- Design goals: predictable latency, high throughput, graceful fallbacks, and minimal per-token cost.

Key components and responsibilities:
- API Gateway / Ingress: TLS termination, auth, per-customer routing policies, initial throttles. Important for RU and quota enforcement.
- Router & Smart Routing: Routes by policy (latency SLO, model family, region, cost tier). Supports fallback policies to compatible model variants.
- Scheduler / Batcher: Continuous batching with priority queuing; local and global schedulers coordinate to satisfy latency SLOs while maximizing GPU utilization.
- Execution Engine: Kernel selection layer (assembly of operator kernels, quantized operator paths, and attention optimizations). Manages KV cache lifecycle per request.
- Cache & KV Store: Prefix cache (request-level) and global KV cache for long running chat sessions; supports TTL, LRU eviction, and consistency guarantees for pinned requests.
- Observability & Tracing: Token-level metrics, per-request trace IDs, and export to the Redwood observability plane.

Ownership and SLA expectations:
- Component owners: Router (team=serving-runtime-router), Scheduler (team=serving-runtime-scheduler), Kernels (team=serving-runtime-exec), Observability/Cache (team=serving-runtime-observability).
- Default SLOs: p95 latency <= 220ms for short-form generation (<=128 tokens) on dedicated pools; availability >= 99.95% for Dedicated and >= 99.5% for hosted tiers.

2) Kernel scheduling and policy guidance

Objectives:
- Maximize GPU utilization without violating latency SLOs.
- Prioritize small, latency-sensitive requests over large batch throughput when required.

Scheduler concepts:
- Per-GPU local scheduler: performs micro-batching and device-level kernel placement. Uses adaptive slotting to mix small and large sequences.
- Global scheduler: allocates requests to pools/pods based on model compatibility, region, and capacity tier. Maintains a global view of headroom and preempts low-priority queued workloads for emergency/SLR traffic.
- Priority classes: real_time (high priority), interactive (medium), batch (low).

Policies and tunables (table):
- "max_latency_slo": "milliseconds configured per route; default 220"
- "max_batch_tokens": "max tokens to include in a device batch; default 4096"
- "min_batch_fill_time_ms": "how long to wait to attempt larger batch; default 5ms for interactive"
- "preemption_threshold_pct": "global queue occupancy above which preemption allowed; default 80%"
- "kv_cache_eviction_policy": "LRU by default; pinned sessions use TTL bypass"

Kernel placement rules:
1. Prefer contiguous memory layout for attention forward & backward kernels to reduce memcpy.
2. For quantized models (4-bit, 8-bit), use quantized execution path kernels; fallback to float kernels only when compatibility or correctness requires.
3. For mixed-sequence batches, split batches by sequence-length buckets and run separate kernel launches to avoid execution divergence.
4. Use fast-fallback kernels on GPUs lacking optimized tensor cores (older generations).

3) Profiling playbooks (CPU/GPU/Memory/KV cache)

When to profile:
- New model onboarding, observed latency regressions (p95 increase > 10%), or increased OOM/eviction rates.

Profiling steps (standard run):
1. Reproduce workload: use benchmark harness with representative prompt sets and traffic distributions (see Benchmarking section).
2. Collect traces: enable request-ID token-level traces and capture GPU traces (nsys) and system metrics (node exporter, DCGM).
3. Hotspot analysis: inspect per-kernel durations, memcpy, kernel queue times, and scheduler wait times.
4. KV cache analysis: measure hit/miss rates, average prefix lengths, and eviction churn.
5. Experiment with knobs: batch sizes, min-fill-time, kernel selection flags, and preemption thresholds. Run A/B comparison.

CLI examples:
- GPU trace capture: nsys profile --sample=none --trace=cuda --output=profile-{{run_id}} nsys-runner -- workload-wrapper
- Runtime trace export: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \n  -X POST https://ingress.redwood.internal/traces/export -d '{"run_id":"{{run_id}}"}'

Common profiling findings and mitigations:
- Symptom: High memcpy times between CPU <-> GPU. Mitigation: Use zero-copy pinned buffers and colocate scheduler with execution node; increase prefetch window.
- Symptom: Long kernel queue wait (kernels queued but not launched). Mitigation: Reduce batch creation rate; split heavy sequences; raise max_batch_tokens if throughput-bound.
- Symptom: KV cache thrash (high eviction). Mitigation: Increase cache size for hotspot model routes, add per-customer cache pinning for hot sessions, or reduce TTLs for low-utility entries.

4) Benchmarking suite and test matrix

Overview:
- The benchmarking suite is the canonical harness used for model onboarding, regression testing, and release validation. Targets: latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, and cost-per-token.

Test matrix (example):
- Model families: small (7B), medium (13B), large (70B float16), quantized variants (int8/4bit).
- Sequence lengths: 16, 64, 128, 512, 1024
- Concurrency profiles: spike (burst of 200 qps), steady (50qps), tail-heavy (90th percentile of long sessions).
- Routing modes: single-GPU, multi-GPU pipeline, offload-to-CPU (for KV heavy paths).

Benchmark steps:
1. Provision test pool (dedicated ephemeral pool) matching target GPU type (A100-40GB, H100, or equivalent).
2. Upload model variant and kernel profile.
3. Run synthetic and replay-based traffic (replay captures stored in /bench/replays).
4. Collect metrics: token latency histograms, GPU metrics (SM utilization, memory bw), and cost telemetry.
5. Compare to baseline: if p95 increased > 7% or throughput decreased > 5% vs baseline, block the release and open a regression ticket.

Golden thresholds (examples):
- p95 latency regression tolerance: 7%
- throughput regression tolerance: 5%
- GPU mem fragmentation: < 8% after warmup

Artifacts produced:
- perf-report-{{model}}-{{gpu}}-{{date}}.json (includes flattened metrics)
- nsys traces and timeline screenshots
- regression check ticket with triage notes and CI link

5) Release notes checklist for runtime changes

Before merging runtime changes to main and promoting to canary/production, complete the checklist:
- [ ] ADR updated if API or scheduling semantics changed
- [ ] Benchmarks run for all supported model classes and quantization variants
- [ ] Profiling traces attached for canary runs
- [ ] Rollout plan documented (percentages, rollback criteria, metric watchlist)
- [ ] Owners & oncall notified (channel: #serving-runtime-release)
- [ ] Canary pass criteria: p95 <= baseline * 1.07 AND error-rate delta < 0.1%

Canary rollout steps (recommended):
1. Deploy to canary pool (1% traffic) for 30 minutes. Monitor latency/cost/path errors.
2. Increase to 5% for 60 minutes if stable.
3. Increase to 25% for 2 hours.
4. Full rollout if no regressions and error budgets remain.

Rollback triggers:
- p95 latency > baseline * 1.12 OR error-rate increase > 0.5% absolute OR any SLO breach for high-priority customers.

6) Known issues and mitigation patterns

Catalog (short list):
- Issue: Intermittent p99 spikes on H100 clusters when mixed float & quantized workloads run.
  - Workaround: Isolate quantized models into dedicated pools and use pre-warmed kernel caches.
- Issue: KV cache evictions during autoscaler events causing chat regressions.
  - Mitigation: Pin hot sessions to sticky instances or snapshot KV to redis-backed warm store before scale-down.
- Issue: Out-of-memory (OOM) on largest models with heavy batching.
  - Mitigation: Reduce max_batch_tokens, enable activation checkpointing for training-derived models, or use pipeline parallel nodes.
- Issue: Higher memcpy overhead on older NIC drivers.
  - Mitigation: Driver upgrade or use RDMA-enabled NICs and upgrade host kernel.

Reporting a new known issue:
1. Create a Confluence incident note and link to the postmortem if needed.
2. Add entry to this document’s known-issues table (include symptoms, impact, workaround, owner).
3. Tag release and notify product & customer success if customer-facing.

7) Runbooks: critical operational procedures

a) Emergency latency regression runbook
1. Triage oncall alert channel and capture current Canary metrics and p95/p99 values.
2. Identify impacted routes and models using per-route traces.
3. Rollback recent runtime or kernel changes if correlated.
4. If rollback not possible, temporarily divert traffic to dedicated low-latency pools or enable degraded-fallback model variant.
5. Open incident in PagerDuty, document steps, and complete post-incident review.

b) Node OOM / GPU OOM recovery
1. Evict low-priority queued tasks: set preemption flag for batch class.
2. Restart failing worker process with --safe-start to warm kernel caches.
3. If persistent, drain node from load, run memcheck, and schedule maintenance window.

c) KV cache cold-start warming
1. Identify hot prefixes from historical traces.
2. Run batch prefix replay to warm prefix/KV caches on target pool before production traffic shift.
3. Monitor hit-rate and evictions for 30 minutes post-warm.
